When Isolde is found savagely killed with barbed wire in her home office, Detective Winston must untangle a web of lies and deception to find out if Samuel or Bernard is responsible.

Detective Winston set down the thick manila folder labeled "Isolde" on the corner of his desk, his mind settling on the details he had scrutinized over coffee and half a dozen cigarettes throughout the night. His next interview would be with Samuel, the paramedic who had attended to their deceased and who was, unfortunately, on duty that day of the murder.

Winston drove to the medical supply store, where his potential suspect was apparently employed. He found Samuel scrubbing down the glass doors of the facility, glimpsing the red-cross logo stitched on his uniform shoulder.

"Samuel?" Winston queried, getting out of his car. 

“Yeah, that’s me," came the tired response. Samuel looked up from his task, tossing a quick glance at the detective’s badge.

“My name’s Detective Winston. I need to speak with you about a few things. Mind if we step inside?” 

“Sure, detective,” Samuel gestured toward the main entrance and Winston followed. 

Once inside, Samuel's persona changed. Winston noticed the way he moved around the shelves, the confidence in his steps. The paramedic knew his way around medical supplies. His extensive training had equipped him with the knowledge to deal with a variety of emergency situations, including trauma inflicted by barbed wire.

A jangling of keys pulled Winston's attention back to Samuel. He was unlocking a storage unit near the far end of the store, revealing shelves lined with a variety of products, including a roll of barbed wire. 

"Just restocking," Samuel explained, but Detective Winston made no response - it wasn't his place to draw conclusions. He pulled out his small notebook from his back pocket, jotting down a few insignificant details before closing it again.

Later that day, Winston visited Isolde’s workspace, noting the appointment book left open on her desk. It showed a visit from Samuel penciled in at a noontime slot, the same day Isolde was murdered. 

Buried under the papers on Isolde's desk, the detective found a DVD labeled "Surgical Errors," - the video evidence of Samuel's medical malpractice. It was clear Isolde had been collecting her evidence against Samuel.

He next met with Isolde’s secretary, who was visibly shaken. "Yes, Detective. I remember confirming Samuel’s appointment." she mentioned, “I believe it was his medical review?"

Winston nodded, making no comment. He reflected upon the video evidence he had found at Isolde’s office. The recording that allegedly held evidence of Samuel's botched surgery had now become more significant.

He returned back to his car, pondering over the details of Samuel's superior who had warned him about the potential job loss and jail time, given his recent errors. 

His last snippet of information had come from a security guard at Isolde's building who had seen Samuel entering her office on the day of the murder.

Winston felt the familiar burn of an overworked mind. But he kept his thoughts at bay as he rounded out his day. The puzzle pieces were often murky, and their connections circumstantial. His job was to find them, and affix them one by one until the whole image revealed itself.

Winston was staring at his murky reflection in the last few drops of coffee. Isolde was dead, strangled in her home office, possibly by her roommate and partner in crime, Bernard. Together, Bernard and Isolde were involved in some mystifying activities, being partners in their dubious affairs while sharing the same living space. 

Winston sighed and thought to his next interview, Bernard. He was next on Winston's list. Known as a cattle rancher in town, Bernard made his living through the ranching business. He was also known for his suspiciously close relationship with Isolde, as they not only shared a living area but were partners in crime.

Upon entering the ranch, Winston noticed Bernard wearing a rugged cowboy hat and a pair of gloves, trying to fix a broken fence. Intriguingly, there was no barbed wire in sight, an important element for a ranch fence. Winston had received a report about missing barbed wire from this very ranch, and here, he was staring at an opened box that should have contained barbed wires for the fence. 

Over a bitter cup of coffee, Winston began his inquiries. "Heard about your Halloween contest victory, Bernard. Hannibal Lecter impersonation, was it?" 

Bernard smiled, his eyes glinting, "Oh yeah, good times. Did an Anthony Perkins one at the last party too, from Psycho." Many at the party overheard Bernard reciting Anthony Perkins' lines with unnerving accuracy.

Winston thought about the strangeness of the situation, a man so obsessed with horror and thrillers, impersonating characters from such genre. Bernard might have been telling the truth, but it was part of Winston's job to consider all possibilities.

Bernard happily divulged how he frequently visits speciality stores to buy all kinds of horror and thriller movies. His eyes lit up with excitement as he spoke about his dedicated room for his extensive movie collection, featuring an array of thrillers with Anthony Perkins' Psycho as the crown jewel.

When Winston asked Bernard for an alibi on the night of Isolde's murder, Bernard reaffirmed he didn't invite anyone else and that he was home alone that night. No neighbors reported any visitors to his residence during the time of the crime. Winston asked Bernard if he noticed anything out of the ordinary during that time, to which Bernard looked puzzled and shook his head.

Winston finished his coffee and made his way towards the door. As he left Bernard's ranch, he noted the puzzling absence of the barbed wire from the fences, Bernard's conspicuous enthusiasm for horror characters, and the deafening silence from the neighbors about any missing barbed wire. The picture was becoming clearer. What conclusions these facts would lead to, that was for a later time. For now, he had to focus on gathering more crucial facts and information about the suspicious circumstances surrounding Isolde's death.

When Roxanne drops dead at the local skate park, the unlikely cause of death being poison from a rare frog, Detective Winston finds himself mired in questioning two intriguing suspects, Stacey and Hector.

In the dim light of his office, detective Winston thumbed through the flight records of one Hector Barbosa, a flight attendant for an international airline. His recent travel logs had him shuttling multiple times to and from South America, the only place where the frog that produces a toxic poison can be found. In just a few weeks of travels, he managed to visit the region several times. Closing the file, Winston grabbed his coat and made his way to Hector’s residence.

Upon arrival at Hector's home, Winston was greeted with an impressive gallery of artwork. Though it seemed grim and somewhat macabre, a theme Hector had expressed enthusiasm for in conversation, Winston had to admit, Hector had talent. Each painting was meticulously detailed and chillingly realistic, with gruesome scenes of death and despair. Hector escorted him through, speaking of his passion and backgrounds; studying biology, specializing in amphibians, particular those native to South America, before taking a recent turn into the fast-paced life as a flight attendant.

Winston moved through the house, noting the unusual abundance of crimson. 

“New project?” He asked. 

“A passion piece...” Hector responded, pointing out to a fresh canvas that sat in the corner, a pot of fresh crimson red paint on an easel next to it that Winston instantly recognized. He'd seen Hector carrying it home from the art supply store earlier.

The following morning Winston placed another visit, this time to the local skate park. Public records indicated both Hector and Roxanne, the victim, frequent activity in this park, perhaps an emblem of their youth, or simply an outlet to unwind. Even here, halfway across the world, Hector was diligent about signing in, a habit that placed him in the vicinity of the crime scene during the murder.

"Hector Barbosa" was clearly listed on the sign-in sheet on the day of the murder. The times matched the timeframe of Roxanne's murder as recorded by the coroner. With no convincing alibi during the time, this only intensified the the suspicion on Hector. 

Winston shoved the paperwork back in his satchel as he stood up to leave. It was time to head back to the office. After taking a last look at the desolate skate park, Winston set a course back to his office. He had a long night of sifting through evidence and connecting the dots ahead of him.

Detective Winston rubbed his temples, going over the case again. It had started with Roxanne, found dead in a skate park one hectic morning. The cause of death had been unusual...poison from a frog. Now his attention was on Stacey, having been seen at the skate park the same day of the murder.

"I did see her there that day...she always came to the same spot, worked on her designs..." the teenage skater he was interviewing stomped his skate on a piece of wood. "Used to be pro, you know, forefront of the game... Then when Roxanne got big, doing all the flashy moves...people started calling her out..."

It was true, Winston reflected as he thanked the skater for his time, Stacey was known in combative sports as an expert. But her athleticism isn't the reason why she fell into his radar. The local pet store owner had a strange tale.

"Yup, she came in the other day and bought a peculiar pet, one of those exotic poison dart frogs... expensive, bright colors..." The pet shop owner, a tattooed man in his fifties, explained. Winston recalled his previous conversation with Stacey. She had openly talked about her trips to rainforests, being an avid hiker, often running into wildlife. She had even mentioned her interest in studying about poison dart frogs.

The day had grown long. Winston returned to the skate park, standing where Stacey would habitually be. Having talked to a number of witnesses who confirmed Stacey’s presence during the same time Roxanne would be...too coincidental he mused. 

"Roxanne liked this spot too...it became her spot after she started ripping off Stacey's designs. Strange, isn't it?" a skateboarder mulled, watching him curiously, "To die in a place where you've stolen so much?"

With Roxanne's sudden rise to stardom, a career that fed off Stacey's unique designs, he had a sense he was close... if only he could outpaint the whole picture.  

"Roxanne didn't care," a girl clad in ripped jeans and a baggy sweatshirt frowned, the anger seeping through her defiant tone, "Even when Stacey begged her to stop, she didn't care...said she'd made them better."

Winston nodded and finally left the park, blending into the late afternoon crowd. This case was becoming increasingly convoluted. But he had an inkling about where the thread might lead... He would continue to pull.

Detective Winston sat at his desk, cradling a cold cup of coffee in his hands. He exhaled deeply, his weary gaze fixed upon the pile of evidence papers laid out in front of him.

Russell. A local poet, renowned for both his artful wordplay and eccentric demeanor. Winston recalled attending a reading Russell held at the local café. Each line made it seem as if the author held intimate knowledge of this mysterious maze.

According to Russell during their encounter, Isabella had threatened to expose a secret to the authorities, a secret that involved some grave mistakes from Russell's past.

As Winston set aside his notebook, a promotional flyer for Russell’s poetry reading found its way into his hands. Intriguingly, this performance had occurred on the very day of Isabella's unfortunate poisoning.

Flipping back through his memories, Winston contemplated on his earlier investigations into Russell's background. The poet had lived a life of adventure before settling into the local town--having trekked to many exotic corners of the world. His fondness for the strange and unique influenced his writing, including several poems dedicated to exotic creatures, such as the poison-arrow frog.

The image depicted Russell, standing proudly next to his illustrious collection of exotic animals, including a concentration of poison-arrow frogs. Word had it that Russell was not only interested in these deadly amphibians but also knowledgeable in extracting their lethal poison.

Winston looked at the facts spread across his desk. Isabella, a seasoned investigator, was to service a search warrant on Travis's tattoo parlor. Winston craved for that tattooed tight-lipped Travis to spill. He was hoping for a lead, a spark, something to light up this utter darkness of evidence.

"Prior to this... investigation, your tattoo shop seemed to be doing pretty well, Travis," Winston clicked his tongue.

In the chilling depths of the swamp, Ricky was found silenced forever by a bottle of bleach, leaving Detective Winston the daunting task of deciphering the lethal motives of the prime suspects, Glenn and Tessa.

In his office, Detective Winston explored the files related to Ricky's murder. The crime scene images were grim; a body dumped in a swamp, a fatal dose of bleach poisoning seemingly the cause. Poor Ricky still wore the glazed-over look of surprise. The thick morass of the swamp had been the final resting place for a man who, not more than a few hours ago, was alive and bound for a visit to his dentist, Glenn.

Winston put away the photos and dialed Glenn's office. A swift answer came from an exhausted receptionist, barely managing to croak out that the clinic was nearing insolvency. She lamented over her situation, without pay for days, and wondering if she'd be paid at all. Winston could feel something wasn't right. He thanked the receptionist and prepared himself for a visit.

Upon arrival to the clinic, the tools of Glenn's trade laid out on a steel tray caught his eye. Among the collection of dental paraphernalia was a large bottle of bleach, no doubt used for sterilizing his instruments. Winston studied the peculiar tall man standing before him, Glenn, a dentist by profession. A professional known to have chosen forensic odontology as a specialty—a pocket of expertise not many in his field would aspire to occupy.

"Now that's an intriguing line of work, Glenn," Winston remarked. Glenn gave a shrug and an almost shy nod before further adding, "I like to keep curious, Detective. I find toxicology talks within dental science forums quite engaging." 

Winston made polite conversation, shifting discussion towards Ricky. "I take it he was in your care recently?"

With a hint of sadness, Glenn responded, "Yes, he only left here yesterday. He had some work required before the holidays."

Before leaving, Winston inquired about Glenn's morning activities, "I hear you're an avid bird watcher, Glenn?"

Laughing, Glenn replied, "Yes, Detective! Nothing like the soft chirping of birds at the break of dawn. I have been birdwatching by, funny enough, the swamp, this very morning."

The detective then revealed a rather puzzling piece of information, he had uncovered during his investigation. "Ricky was found dead in the very swamp, you were birdwatching today, killed by bleach," he stated matter-of-factly.

Glenn looked genuinely shell-shocked; fear slowly seeping into his gaze. Sensing his discomfort, Winston decided to leave him with one last piece of information, "One more thing, Glenn. Ricky had you listed as the beneficiary on his life insurance policy." Winston held out the document from his satchel, showing Glenn the listed beneficent's name was indeed his.

"And just last week you mentioned the high monetary benefits that such a policy could bring in, didn't you, Glenn?" Winston added, watching the shock travel from Glenn's face to his very feet.

Not waiting for an answer, Winston turned and left the dental clinic, leaving Glenn to his thoughts.

Winston wrinkled his nose at the pungent odour of the swamp. Someone had found Ricky's body among the overgrown weeds and murky waters. An unfortunate end he mused, standing within walking distance of the local prison nearby. As he prepared to interview a potentially connected party — Tessa, a chemistry teacher turned inmate, he ran over the facts in his mind. 

Her current occupation as a cleaner in the prison's system gave her access to various supplies, cleaning supplies in particular. There were rumours of her unauthorized experiments involving bleach which had spiralled her into trouble once. Moreover, she worked on a farm near this very swamp.

Walking through the steel encased hallways of the prison, Winston arrived at Tessa's workspace. Finding her face damp with sweat, the persistent clang of her efforts to clean reverberated in the small and dank concrete space. She paused when he called her, "Tessa," Winston began, his tone crisp and official. "I'm detective Winston. I understand you taught chemistry before your unfortunate incarceration." 

"Yeah, I did. Is my knowledge of chemistry a crime now too?" Tessa paused,-looking at him expectantly. 

"Investigating a crime scene, Ricky's body was found in a nearby swamp," Winston continued ignoring her comments. "Awfully close to the prison farm you've been working on."

She made no visible reaction to the news. Then crossed her arms, furrowing her brows. "What's that got to do with any of this? And why should I know him? There are hundreds of prisoners passing through these cells..."

Ignoring her defensive stance, Winston targeted a more interesting topic, "Word has it you've been passionately sharing some rather unique dreams with your cell mates?" 

Tessa stared at Winston blankly, and then nodded. "Yeah, dreams... dreams of dying. Dreams of new beginnings. Awfully real. I don't know why, but I felt compelled to share them, almost eagerly. Figured I needed some context to these vivid dreams, so I started visiting the prison library often."

"In the sections about spiritualism, death rituals, and reincarnation, I believe? Parts of the sections involving death and the afterlife?" Winston queried.

"Yeah, that's right. It soothes me, somehow," Tessa shrugged, resuming her duties.

Leaving her to her cleaning, he walked away, the vestiges of the swamp carrying a far more sinister weight now.

For Detective Winston, a seasoned investigator who had seen every shade of human nature, the affair of Ricky's murder seemed unusual. He detested the musky smell of the swamps where Ricky's body was found that same day. But of course, the repugnance a crime scene induces is not a criterion to be considered in investigations. 

His letters of introduction remarked that he would be received by Glenn, a local dentist. As Winston rounded upon the dental clinic, he couldn't fail to notice the tell-tale smell of sterilizing bleach that hung heavily in the air.

"Morning Doctor," Winston said as he walked into the clinic.

"Good Morning, How can I help you?" replied Glenn.

"My name is Winston. I am investigating the death of one Ricky," he explained.

Glenn visibly shuttered at the mention of Ricky's name, "I had seen him recently for a root canal."

Winston wasn't too surprised by this. Many victims' last known location turned out to be places where they had felt safe. He made a mental note of it but didn't engage in any further discussion about Ricky.

He noticed a desktop computer nearby where a dental science forum was open. Topics on toxicology and possible risk factors danced on the screen. "Is that what you were doing before I walked in?" Winston mused aloud.

"I was catching up on some forensic odontology discussions. It's my area of specialty," Glenn explained, sounding unusually enthusiastic about the subject. 

Tickets to Ricky's funeral were spread out on Glenn's desk, indicating that he'd likely be offering his last respects to the deceased individually. The dentist, a loner by appearance, never invites anyone to his remote house where he lives all by himself. This he didn't strike Winston as the kind to mingle at a social gathering.

Winston inquired about Glenn's whereabouts for most of the day Ricky was murdered, to which Glenn quickly responded, "I was out birdwatching at the swamp."

"But I heard you live in that isolated homestead," Winston said, diverting the conversation towards Glenn's personal life, "You don't usually invite anyone over?"

This time, Glenn didn't just show discomfort. He stammered and went pale. Clearly, his anxiety was rising at each personal question, 
and in an effort to divert the conversation, he interjected, "Do you know that prolonged use of teeth whitening treatment can cause oral cancer?" Winston was taken by surprise at the sudden change in conversation but chose not to question it any further. 

With that, his introduction to Glenn was over and his investigation continued.

Detective Winston pulled up to the prison, parking his car between the tall, barbed wire fences. Beyond them, he could see a swamp, the murky water shimmering with heat. Footsteps echoed through the sterile, concrete halls as he made his way inside, passing groups of colorfully uniformed prisoners on their way to and from various responsibilities. 

Brushing off some of the dust still clinging onto her orange jumpsuit, Tessa sat in the visiting room, the corners of her mouth curled into a hint of a smile. 

"Tessa," Winston began, "You work here on farms, correct?"

She nodded, crossing her arms over her chest, "Yeah, that's correct. We've got a swamp nearby too."

Winston wrote something down, answering with a nonchalant "Mmhhm."

"And before prison... you were a high school chemistry teacher, weren't you?"

"Yeah,” she grumbled, “From Bunsen burners to mop buckets."

"So, your current job here... cleaning, right?" to which Tessa confirmed. 

"And in turn, they provide you the cleaning supplies?"

"Yep,” she mused, “A mop, bucket, soap, gloves... bleach. Everything a good custodian ought to need." 

Winston scooted himself forward a bit, "You were disciplined once for using bleach incorrectly, right?"

Her face turned expressionless. "That was years ago. Nothing but some harmless experiments." Tessa asserted.

As minutes rolled into hours, the conversation moved onto the victim, Ricky. Ruffling in his seat, Winston asked about the dwindling debt between Tessa and Ricky. 

"He couldn't just wait, huh? Always pestering about the damn debt. I tried to repay him, but it just never seemed enough." Tessa confessed, clenching her fist, "He even threatened me over it."

Underneath the fluorescent lights, Winston could see her distress - unable to keep up with Ricky's demands despite her financial limitations. 

Remembering his autopsy briefing, Winston knew Ricky was found in the very swamp near the prison's farm. Perhaps, Tessa knew something...

"Ricky's body was found near the swamp, past the farm." Winston stated.

A flicker of shock passed through Tessa's eyes before her face returned back to its hardened, impassive state. She may not have expected anyone would find him, or for the news to reach her this quickly. "Near the farm, within the walking distance he murmured..."

He thanked her for talking and left, leaving Tessa alone in the visiting room. 

As he walked back through the dense crowd of prisoners, past the pungent smell of bleach cleaning the hallways, Winston realized, this was going to be a difficult case to crack. A life lost over a debt, and the swamp held many secrets yet to reveal.

“Detective,” Eddie said, quelling the enthusiasm in his tone. 

“Glad to see you can take time away from your practice,” Winston said casually.

Winston moved on. " I heard from Letti, she’d invited you for a song recording at her isolated mountain cabin, which you're staying at for the duration of the recording."

Eddie nodded. “Yes, it was a wonderful opportunity. Her mountain cabin is beautifully isolated, which makes it an inspiring place especially when you're used to the solitude of camping.”

"I heard you're someone who enjoys a robust collection of wildlife taxidermy," Winston shifted the topic.

Eddie’s face lit up, “Yes, I’ve got a whole room full of specimens at my place, even from endangered species. Interesting how life becomes art with death.”

The interview was interrupted by a growing chorus of fans demanding another performance. Eddie nodded to Winston, picked up his machete, and slipped away. The very same machete he used during his camping trips for safety, now became a prop in his spectacle. He showed the audience his machete tricks, with cheers accompanying each swift, practiced movement.

Winston withdrew from the place, drowned out by the cheering crowd. He left for the isolation of the night, knowing that his work here wasn't nearly done.

Winston pondered over the details of the case. The victim, Letti, had shared with friends about finding documents that implicated her godmother, Delilah, in illicit activities. She had even voiced her intent to go public, starting with confronting Delilah directly. Witnesses reported the last time anyone saw her, it was when Letti walked right into Delilah's cabin with an unflinching resolve. That forced his hand, leading him straight to Delilah's secluded dwelling.

Perched in a rural area with few other houses for company, the cabin was nestled within a copse of trees. As he approached, he saw Delilah outside. Delilah, who was the sole occupant of the cabin known to neighbours, was regularly seen practising with a machete for security purposes. True to the reports, there she was, swinging the machete with a practiced flair, the sun igniting its path before it landed in the trunk of a tree, vibrating under the force of her strike. Even a novice could tell she was someone who knew her way around a blade.

Having verified her identity, Winston started his interrogation casually, focusing on her peculiar hobby. The queries were about her familiarity with the machete and how she had become so skilled. Delilah responded, her accent echoing with local tones, "I've been using a machete since I was a teenager." She continued, reliving her past, "Father taught me. I've won a few of the local competitions, too. Helps living alone out here, one needs to keep sharp."

Winston noted down her history with the weapon and the regular practise for security. He then moved on to discuss Letti. "Did Letti come here often?" he asked.

She confirmed, "Letti did come often, yes. The last time she came was yesterday." Her face revealed a shift in emotion, recognising the motive behind Winston's questioning. Being keen, he paid heed but continued to be nonchalant.

He then prodded about her lifestyle. "You live all alone out here?"

With a nod, Delilah confirmed the solitary lifestyle as she retrieved her machete from the tree. Winston, in the following silence, surveyed the lush woodland around the cabin — offering privacy and seclusion. They marked a stark dichotomy between peace and potential criminal activity within an authoritarian mind like him.

Trying to read any hint of reaction, he brought up Letti's concern. "Your goddaughter," Winston started, "She was worried about you. She found some documents and directly confronted you about some suspicious activities. She even threatened to make it public."

Delilah went rigid, her gaze darting toward the cabin. Her cabin – Letti's statements to her friends made it clear. Winston caught the twitch in her eyes but decided not to press further. His main inquiries were done, and the cloak of night began to envelop the landscape. However, he didn't leave empty-handed. The information gleaned from Delilah filled in gaps of Letti's allegations, driving him closer to the incident's truth on the fateful night. In a bustling office, a mundane bottle of bleach becomes a lethal weapon, leading to the chilling murder of Murray; it's up to the sharp-minded Detective Winston to navigate through a web of deceit spun by Chris and Gloria, the enigmatic suspects.

The rain was lightly tapping against the window of Detective Winston's office as he examined his notes. His latest case involved a peculiar victim, Murray, who was fond of working alone during the twilight hours in his office. The cause of death was a strange one - bleach ingestion.

After nightfall, Winston's steps echoed in the office building as he sought out his next interviewee. Emerging from a nondescript door labelled "Rehearsal", the sound of dancers practicing halted abruptly. Winston found himself amongst Gloria's dominion.

“Ms. Gloria, could I have a moment of your time?” Winston asked, interrupting her choreography.

“Every second counts, Detective... My rehearsals always seem to go overtime,” Gloria replied, her voice resounding in the empty practice space. Around her, a set of costumes lined the room, each one carefully cleaned. Gloria had a reputation for maintaining the utmost hygiene in her costumes.

Winston remarked, "It's unusual to see a dance studio without a security camera. The owners not concerned about break-ins?"

“Well, they leave matters of security to us... How could I help, Detective?” Gloria pushed aside her rehearsal props, which included a curious bleach bottle among her personal belongings, providing Winston a chair in her living quarters in the rehearsal building. Given her late-night practices, she had repurposed a portion of the room to serve as her personal living space.

In her living space, an enormous filing cabinet stood imposingly, filled to the brim with newspaper clippings. Winston could tell she was fond of keeping up with recent events. Also, the sheer size of the cabinet suggested it might be Gloria’s version of a living room.

"I see you have a large filing cabinet in your living quarters, Gloria. That’s quite full of newspaper clippings." Winston commented, pointing to the open drawer.

"Ah, Detective, I like to stay informed... I make it a point to read through every obituary in the early morning. A peculiar morning ritual, I know...," Gloria replied, confirming her subscription to every local newspaper.

"You certainly seem to research chemicals, too,” Winston observed, his eye having been caught by the organized array of chemical notations and formulas that were punctuating her choreography notes.

“Absolutely," Gloria animatedly replied, quickly adding, "For example, bleach is highly toxic when ingested. It's commonly used for maintaining the hygiene of the costumes.” 

Winston stood up to leave, thanking Gloria for her time. "So do you use this office year-round?"

"No, only for late-night practices. And I believe Murray also preferred afterhours here," Gloria offered.

"Thank you for your time, Gloria."

“Detective, are you sure you have all the information you need?” Gloria asked, escorting him to the door.

“I believe I do. I’ll be in touch,” Winston nodded, stepping back out into the dim-lit alley.

Winston sat in the hard plastic chair outside the office of Chris, the coach of the office's intramural sports leagues. The location seemed like an unlikely place for a murder, but Murray had indeed collapsed dead in his office several buildings over from ingesting a poisonous substance, a terrible surprise considering Murray typically avoided the recreational facilities of the office.

The door cracked open, and Chris invited Winston in. The office was small but spacious enough to hold stacks of sports equipment, training manuals and a variety of cleaning agents that he included as part of his coaching supplies - everything from towels to a close-to-empty bottle of bleach. Winston looked at the bleach and couldn't help but recollect the unfortunate death of Murray, caused by poison.

The two men sat on either side of the desk cluttered with paper-work and game plans. "Murray?" Chris grimaced as he spoke out the name of the victim, a surprising response from an individual not typically associated with the inter-office politics.

Winston cleared his throat, initiating the conversation. "When did you last see him, Chris?"

"Funny you'd ask. Just yesterday, in his office. Over a decision in the final game, you know." Chris's voice grew noticeably cooler.

Winston recalled the chatter at the water-cooler about last week's defeat in the championship game. The stakes high, the loss did not sit well with the team or Chris, as Winston observed from the stern look on the coach's face. There had been confrontations, Winston had heard, and the echo of an argument -- Murray's decision suddenly seemed to favor the rival team.

"Everyone was... upset," Winston found the right word, "about the decision. The last match was important, wasn't it?"

"More than just a game, wasn’t it Detective?" Chris's evasive reply wrapped around his rising passion for the job. The loss was more personal, Winston noted.

“You’re here during the day, right?” Winston asked, looking for a confirmation.

“Yes, sir. My coaching matches the office's regular hours,” Chris replied.

“Your duties - it must be more than throwing balls and yelling at players.” It was Winston’s turn to lighten up the mood.

“Funny, Detect. I’m responsible for equipment and supply maintenance. And trust me, yanking up fifty-pound weights and keeping the towels and bottles clean and safe - it ain’t no walk in the park.”

"Safe? Like using cleaning products perhaps,” Winston stated, looking right at the supplies Chris kept in his office.

“Sure. You never know when something spills. Have to keep it all clean and safe," Chris echoed.

Winston recollected an incident from the past where a young office athlete under Chris's coaching had ingested cleaning fluid, mistaken for water no less, and had an unpleasantly grim hospital visit. The echo of that incident reverberating in the present, with Murray's poisoning almost felt like a devious pattern, thought Winston.

"Wouldn’t want another upset tummies, would we?” Winston rose from the chair, leaving Chris with a thoughtful stare.

"No, we wouldn’t, Detective."

Winston left the office, running over the conversation in his mind as he remembered the empty bottle of bleach in the corner of Chris’s office. There was certainly more to uncover; the echoes of past and present were too loud to ignore.

When a friendly game of paintball turns fatal with the shocking grenade murder of Ana, seasoned Detective Winston sets out to uncover the hidden truths that lie behind the friendly faces of Troy and Bethany.

Detective Winston counted his steps as he moved between the splattered remains of what was once a thriving paintball field. His thoughts lingered on Ana’s abrupt violence.

Official reports had solidified that aside from the victim, only one other person had been present that tragic night. Troy- the community’s spearheading missionary and the contender in that ill-fated paintball match, was reported to make an unusually early exit, shortly after the deafening explosion that had claimed Ana's life.

“I believe you can, Troy.” Winston replied, deciding to keep the conversation light. “Must be tough work, serving in war-torn areas.”

Winston was sitting in his car, gazing at the misty country road that led to Gordon's farm. Bad news was often paired with a country farm, but today was particularly grave - A death at the chalet, a bear trap, and a farmer named Gordon.

Winston slowly climbed out of the car as he neared the farmhouse - a large wooden structure isolated in the distant country land, adjacent to a somber cemetery. The only cemetery in town, he thought. Isolated, just like Gordon, its only neighbor who immigrated here with no known family. Gordon had landed there, growing crops, breeding animals, keeping up a farm.

He walked up the pathway onto the farm, noticing the creaking wooden sign that read 'Gordon's Hunting Supplies'. It was evident that Gordon was more than just a standard farmer. The sign was riddled with buckshot. 'Bear problems,' Winston thought to himself as he made his way to the front door. 

Gordon was sitting on a rickety wooden stool as Winston made his approach. He was weathered from years of outdoor work and his eyes carried an unmistakable lonesome pain. His fists were gripped around a wooden handle, tapping rhythmically onto the dry farm soil. He was tense.

"Gordon?" Winston quietly asked. The man nodded in response keeping his gaze fixed intently on the horizons towards the cemetery. 

Having heard about Gordon's regular evening walks towards the cemetery, Winston tried to carefully navigate the conversation towards Harry. 

"Heard you folks had quite a fuss at the farmer's market recently?" The old farmer barely reacted, still lost in his world. 

"Took away your best customer, did he?" added Winston, trying to draw Gordon out. He was referring to the fact that their recent altercation was born out of Harry winning an award for his agricultural products - a feat that Gordon declared was a result of favoritism and had led to his sales dropping.

Minutes of silence passed before Gordon finally spoke haltingly, "Harry cost me my sales, my livelihood... Those people chose his products over mine."

Then, as if realizing he'd said too much, Gordon hastily added, "But that's all he took. I got no hard feelings.”

Winston carefully listened but made no attempt to comfort Gordon or press the matter further. He took one final look at the brooding farmer, jotting down the conversation in his notepad.

Leaving the stoic and isolated farmer behind, Winston walked back to his car, the image of Gordon gazing over his desolate farm, framed by the town cemetery slowly fading away in the rearview mirror. His evening walk later would follow the usual path towards the cemetery. Gordon might be an immigrant here, but the cemetery and the isolation made him a local... and a person of interest.

Winston stood by the window in the chalet, gazing at the dense forest that surrounded the remote building. The last golden rays of the setting sun were piercing through the firs, illuminating the disturbingly peaceful crime scene where Harry met his end.

"Winston." His name was uttered by a bulky figure standing at the edge of the woods. He turned to see Dexter approaching him, his hulking silhouette cast in shadows by the setting sun.

"Evening." Winston greeted. "You're Dexter, right?"

"That's right." Dexter responded, a friendly smile replacing his creased frown. "I'm guessing you're here about Harry."

"We'll have to speak about that." Winston confessed. "Did you often hunt around these parts?"

"Every chance I get." Dexter nodded, glancing back at the woods. "The owner and I... we're close, see. Been hunting together for years. Learned a lot about traps and hunting methods in that time. He's generous too, lets me use the chalet pretty often."

"This a bear trap?" Winston gestured to the congealing pool of blood around the sprung trap. 

"Yeah, standard issue for anyone serious about hunting." Dexter confirmed, casting a wary glance at the gruesome sight. "I keep quite the collection actually."

"Did you and Harry have any bad blood?"

"He disrespected me... but that's public knowledge." Dexter replied, his smile not reaching his eyes this time. His hands clenched as he added, "Mocked my faith, right in front of everyone at a ceremony."

"Your faith is important to you?"

"Faith defines me, Winston." Dexter said emphatically, "It's everything to me."

"We'll be in touch." Winston assured, nodding before he turned to leave, leaving Dexter standing by the chalet, the scarlet sunset painting a vibrant backdrop to the grim crime scene.

Winston, drizzly and cold from the rain, squinted at the farmhouse across the gloomy countryside. The hunting shop sign creaking in the wind was a well-known fixture having Gordon's name inscribed in bold on the top. Winston knew very well that the shop was run by Gordon, who was as good a supplier of hunting equipment as he was a farmer. The murder of Harry, now known in newspapers as "The Chalet Bear Trap Murder," had to be untangled.

In front of Winston, a rough-faced man, smeared with sweat and dust from his work at both the shop and the farm, set to work, carrying feed bags to the barn. It was Gordon, the local farmer in question.

"Hello, Gordon," - Winston greeted him.

"Howdy, got no time to chat. Gotta feed the animals before the weather worsens. These parts, we got some bear problems," - Gordon grunted in response.

Catching a break, Winston moved towards the subject. "I heard you had some form of disagreement with Harry at the farmer's market a while back."

Scoffing, Gordon refused to meet his gaze. "Sure, we had words... I wasn't selling much, and he was selling everything. Fella won an award recently for his agricultural products while the market for my products was going under."

"You blame Harry for that?" - Winston asked, laying the facts bare.

"Goddam right I do..." - Gordon muttered, throwing a dirty sack onto a pile.

"Where were you at the time Harry was killed, Gordon?"

The farmer dusted his hands, meeting Winston's gaze with defiance. "I was here, at the farm. All day. You can ask anyone around."

“As for the chalet where poor Harry met his end..." - Winston started.

“Yeah, Harry was at my chalet. It’s my property, and I’m the who decides who can or can't access it." - Gordon interrupted, more flustered now.

"Did you see anyone else around that day?"

"Nope. Quiet as a mouse that day, just the bears and me."

After that, silence fell over the now dark homestead. Winston considered the facts, the countryside, farm, bears, the market, the struggling sales, it all called for further investigation. But for now, he just tipped his hat and walked back to his car under the drizzling rain, leaving a brooding Gordon to his work.

As the sheer size of the chalet murder scene could overwhelm a lesser detective, Winston, stood firm. The victim, Harry, was a known critic within the food industry. His sharp tongue had a penchant for landing him in a hot stew of trouble. This time, it would seem, there was a rogue ingredient he just couldn't swallow.

Winston strolled over to Dexter, a known acquaintance of Harry's and an avid food enthusiast himself. The man's love for fine cuisine was matched only by his fervour for his religion.

"Evening, Dexter," Winston began. "How are you holding up?"

"I'm doing okay... under the circumstances." Dexter wasn't the most expressive despite his harsh critiques.

"I heard Harry was very open about his thoughts on your religious beliefs," Winston continued.

Dexter sighed, "Yes, he publicly mocked my faith during an event. Disrespectful, but that was just Harry."

"Dexter," Winston turned back to him, "I noticed a photograph of you and Tony the Tooth having dinner together surfaced on social media. Where were you the night of Harry's death?"

"I... I was there, having dinner with Tony, known to his friends as 'Tony the Tooth,' I've recently learned."

Winston paused at the mention of that name. Tony the Tooth’s reputation proceeded him. Known as a racketeer and money launderer, his guilty verdict in a recent court case was infamous. Dexter's association with him, especially in a photograph in a restaurant notoriously frequented by other criminals, only bred more suspicion.

Changing tactics, Winston delved into Dexter's rural interests. Dexter's love for hunting was no secret to the community; he was often seen in the woods around the outskirts of the town. Dexter was not only known for his hobby of collecting hunting equipment but also for his knowledge of various hunting techniques. One of the common pieces of equipment in his collection was bear traps, which he frequently used in the woods. Dexter was often seen studying these traps, enhancing his understanding of them.

"Care to show me your hunting gear?" Winston suddenly asked, catching him off guard.

"Sure, I guess," Dexter replied tensely. He led the way to a shed, where hunting equipment including rifles and the commonly used bear traps littered the floor and walls.

"It's quite the collection," Dexter added, trying to read Winston's face.

Winston, however, didn't respond. He scribbled down a few more notes before thanking Dexter for his time and heading back to his car. His head was awash with the evening's revelations, notably Dexter's disrespect and his surprising dinner partner.

In the haunting echoes of a cinema hall, Tracy's life was abruptly silenced by the grim stroke of a meat cleaver, leaving Detective Winston grappling with a chilling mystery and two elusive suspects - Nicole and Gloria.

Winston, standing behind the caution tape, looked at the cinema marquee. He allowed the scene to imprint itself in his mind before he would venture inside to inspect the crime scene. A murder at the movies was a rarity. But what was even more unusual was the murder weapon used: a meat cleaver.

Reviewing the details of the case once more, Winston thought about some key players involved. Undeniably traceable was Gloria, a hardcore fan of the rock band 'The Butchers', known by everyone and even herself in interviews, as a groupie. She had also confessed in one such media interaction that she was crazy about taxidermy, a hobby brought to life in her house.

Leaving the crime scene, Winston made his way to Gloria's house in the fading evening sun. Upon entering Gloria's home, he found himself in a museum of morbid curiosity. From the ceiling to the floor, taxidermied animals filled the house with glassy eyes reflecting in the dim light, a testimony to her hobby.

Among her collection, he noticed a recent addition - a rare bird, its exotic colors momentarily catching his gaze. Bob, the local bird dealer, had already confirmed its purchase by Gloria.

Winston inquired about her whereabouts the previous night.

"Well, I was at the movie premiere, of course," Gloria responded. "I, along with Tracy, went to the double event. The Butchers premiered their new music video during the movie. And well, you couldn't expect me to miss that, now could you? I follow every event they put up and not just because I'm a fan. Because I am in love with the lead singer, and yes I'm saying it."

Winston let the information sink in.

"Well... isn't it true that Tracy, the victim, was planning to go public with an affair?" Winston asked.

A momentary flicker passed in Gloria's eyes. "Yes... I know about that," Gloria confessed. "She was dating the lead singer, the poor man. She wanted to reveal everything, destroy everything."

With that, Winston left Gloria's house with more questions buzzing in his head. He got back into his car, piecing together the intricate web of clues this case held. The concert that the Butchers were supposed to play after the movie was now going to be remembered for all the wrong reasons.

Deep in thought, Winston flipped through the photographs of the movie theatre crime scene, when his partner handed him an envelope. A DVD from the theatre's CCTV records, witnessing every unscripted moment at the theatre that did double-duty, not just as a place to showcase films, but also as a distinctive setting for unorthodox weddings, just like the one Tracy had intended to have. Eyewitnesses at the scene confirmed Nicole's presence at the theatre during the murder. The records would be viewed later.

His current priority was to interrogate Nicole, the esteemed wedding planner, the woman whose entire reputation and business were built on her success in this field. By an unfortunate coincidence, she had been at the theatre when Tracy was murdered, not just as a cinema enthusiast, but as the individual orchestrating Tracy's movie-themed wedding at the same theatre.

"Nice place you've got here," Winston observed as he ventured into Nicole's office, its grandeur coupled with an array of movie posters illustrating her success in planning film-themed weddings.

"Well, Detective, events won't plan themselves," Nicole said, with a small, tight smile. "Tracy hired me for one of my elaborate movie-themed weddings. She was drawn to the unusual."

Surveying the space, he noticed it was not only amassed with wedding supplies but also held a vast array of kitchen equipment. Nicole had been responsible for preparing the meat at several events as evident from the professional cleavers that took center stage amongst the kitchenware. One of them catching his eye; a meat cleaver.

"On food responsibility as well?" Winston asked.

"Indeed. Delivering comprehensive experiences is the goal. Every specification matters, including the banquet," Nicole imparted. "My past as a culinary student till being a wedding planner helped shape that. I even received professional training in meat preparation."

"Interesting," Winston murmured, quickly connecting two points - Nicole's past culinary training and Tracy's murder weapon, a meat cleaver.

"Rumor has it that you made a considerable blunder at Tracy's wedding," Winston broached. "Word on the street is that Tracy was so embarrassed she was looking to file a malpractice suit against you.”

"A minor miscalculation. No one is perfect, detective. However, Tracy blew it out of proportion," Nicole responded, her face growing somber.

Observing her seemingly unflustered demeanor, Winston mused on her case. He knew a large scale malpractice suit could irreparably harm a professional's reputation. For someone like Nicole whose entire business relied on her successful track record as a wedding planner, it could be a fateful blow. 

Before confronting her head-on, he decided to examine the perspectives of the eyewitnesses and the CCTV footage. His eyes strayed to the cold, gleaming steel of the meat cleaver amidst Nicole's kitchen equipment. This reminded him of Tracy, and he made himself a promise: he would find justice for her.

"Ms. Nicole?" Detective Winston asked, stepping to one side to permit a waiter carrying a tray of canapés to pass by. They were at the wedding of another one of Nicole's clients, and the venue was abuzz with celebrations.

"I don't have much time, detective," she began, a practiced, friendly tone to her voice. "Please. Tell me this isn't about the court case. Losing something significant like the case with Tracy... it could irreparably harm my reputation."

"What?" The color drained from Nicole's face. She guided him to a quieter corner of the venue, away from the prying ears of her bustling staff. She pulled herself back together and fell right back into the professional demeanor she wore earlier. "See, detective, I’m not just a wedding planner, my whole business is built on my reputation for successful weddings and food catering services too.”

"Hmm," Winston grumbled non-committally as he pocketed his notebook, faintly grinning at her bemused expression. "Let's just say it's a detective's intuition."

Standing alone amidst the bustle, he allowed himself a moment to ponder. Nicole, the wedding planner who found herself in a pickle with her disgruntled client, Tracy. Her recently acquired skill in meat preparation, and a significant part of her services being dedicated to it. How she wielded her set of cleavers, meat cleaver included, with practiced precision. And her annoying habit of checking the obituaries. Nicole's reputation and entire business rested on the premise of her being a successful wedding planner. He glanced back at the array of shiny utensils Nicole had at his disposal. Truly a fascinating case.

Detective Winston rested his worn leather shoes on the edge of the desk, as he thumbed through the file regarding the murder of Tracy. A murder at a movie theater during a rock band’s music video premiere was a first for him. 

'Save for the worst', his grandfather always used to remind him while teaching poker.

The band in question was called “The Butchers”, and they were supposedly somewhere around the murder scene. He found the name intriguing, as he looked through photographs of the band shooting a promotional video at a local butcher shop, “Slice & Dice.”

He then examined interviews given by witnesses and people involved. That's when he came across the name 'Gloria'. She was an ardent fan of “The Butchers”, attending all their shows. “Slice & Dice”, he noted from her employment record, was also her place of work.

"Miss Gloria, I believe the band was slated to perform after the movie?" he asked, leaning forward.

"Yes. Everyone was eagerly waiting for it," she replied, her eyes fixed on a picture of the lead singer.

"All of you were present at the premiere; you, Tracy, the band. Is that correct?" 

"Yes, I... I never miss their shows," she confessed.

"I see, Miss Gloria," he responded, "The Butchers have a committed fan base."

Suddenly, he asked, "Were you aware of Tracy’s intention to reveal her affair with the lead singer?”

Taken by surprise, she nodded and softly said, “Yes.”

"So you were in love with him too, Miss Gloria?” Winston asked. Gloria looked at him in shock but after a few moments of silence, nodded again. 

"Thank you for your time, Miss Gloria,” Winston said, standing up to leave.

As he exited “Slice & Dice,” he noticed a pile of promotional meat cleavers right by the door. They were a symbol of the band, he deduced, something they handed out to fans at their events.

Regardless of the peculiar nature of this case, he had to remain focused. There were facts to be processed, people to be questioned, and justice awaited. After all, he had a solid hand and now, it was time to play it.

In the aftermath of a devastating home explosion that claims the life of Angela, seasoned Detective Winston hones in on two prime suspects: Patrick and Alvin.

Detective Winston grimly regarded the charred remains of Angela's home, considering the pieces of evidence. Home explosions were not commonly dealt with in his line of work, though he knew very well that such explosives were often used in demolitions. 

With such knowledge, he was reminded of a local surfing instructor who also took part in an unconventional part-time job that would put him in frequent touch with explosives, training weekly on handling and disposal. This wasn't his usual surfing job but his part-time work as a demolition worker. This was no doubt, Patrick.

Finding his interview notes with Patrick, Winston decided it was time to speak with him again. Winston had known Patrick through his work, not because he surfed but because of his other role in demolition, an occupation that naturally involved a great deal of work with explosives.

Winston set off to the beach in search of Patrick, eventually spotting him as he was patiently teaching a young boy how to ride the waves. "Patrick!" he called out to him.

Recognizing Winston, the man navigated back to shore on his surfboard with a practised ease. "Detective Winston," he greeted, wiping the saltwater off his face. "How can I help you?"

"Just a few questions," Winston replied. He opened his notebook to a page of carefully penned notes about Patrick's financial troubles. "I heard that you've been having some trouble... getting into a failed investment, left with a sizeable debt?”

Patrick's face tightened, but he nodded in admission. "That's right. Lost all my savings, even borrowed a huge amount from Angela, but the investment went under."  

"Angela had been lending you money, huh?" Winston asked, wanting to confirm the loan from Angela. "And you haven't been able to pay her back because you lost your main job?"

“That’s correct, detective,” the man answered, his face grim with the weight of his troubles.

"Angela ever threaten to, oh, say, call the police on you?" Winston casually asked, inspecting the worn strap of his watch.

Patrick hesitated before finally sighing and admitting, "Yes, she did. More than once. I guess she had enough of my money problems and empty promises."

Somewhat satisfied, Winston took down the latest confession. Glancing around the beach, he then asked, "You were around Angela's house the evening of the explosion?" 

"Detective... it's not far from here, I often pass by when I go home," Patrick replied, his face tense at the questioning.

"Well, nobody else was around her place at that time," Winston mentioned, "Just an interesting fact."

In the awkward silence that followed, Winston then asked about the part that bothered him the most. "You use explosives much with your part-time work and your frequent training, Patrick?" 

Patrick seemed to straighten, “I have, yes, in controlled environments and with appropriate permits.” His voice was firm, perhaps a little defensive.

"Right, part of the job, I guess," Winston nodded, closing his notebook. Not another word was spoken between them as he walked away, leaving a nervous Patrick behind.

Winston gave a slow pull from his coffee as he sat across from Alvin, the typically even-tempered delivery man whose vehicle was loaded and ready for his daily route through town. Alvin's calm demeanor had earned him a reputation among the townsfolk as reliable, if not a tad peculiar due to his habit of having his lunch beside graves. 

Alvin's reliable routine encompassed the entire town including the cemetery - on today's agenda, he'd be stopping at Angela's to drop off a package. His daily routines had put him on a first-name basis with Angela, as she always made a point to personally welcome him into her home when he arrived with her deliveries. 

"So Alvin, any big plans for today?" Winston asked, making casual conversation. "Oh yes," Alvin replied, a spark in his usually placid eyes. "I've just bought a vintage Victorian-era coffin from an auction. Also, I am picking up some decommissioned explosives from a contact in the military. They're for a historical display I'm working on. Can't wait to get both set up in the living room."

This interest didn't surprise Winston. Alvin was known to frequent antique shops, specifically those that boasted a range of mortuary relics. It was odd, sure, but Alvin being odd was one of the few things that gave him character. 

"Did you know Angela?" he asked Alvin in a low tone, a hint of suspicion in his voice. Alvin nodded, "Yes. I deliver her packages regularly. Also," he said after a pause, "I was due to deliver a package to her today."

That tidbit of information Winston knew. Angela was home that day to get her package, but she had not been prepared for what the delivery contained. The investigation revealed that the fatal box delivered to Angela's house was filled with explosives, and the only man who Winston knew had any experience with such devices was Alvin.

Alvin’s past in the military gave him the exposure and knowledge about explosives that most people didn't have. It was common knowledge in their tight-knit community where personal histories were difficult to conceal. While this knowledge alone didn’t constitute evidence, it was certainly one fact of many that were swirling around in Winston’s head.

As Alvin got up to leave, Winston gave him a tight smile, "I hope you enjoy setting up your new coffin and your explosives display, Alvin," he said. “Thank you,” Alvin replied, oblivious to any undercurrent in the conversation, his calm demeanor never wavering. 

Winston finished his coffee, his mind firmly focused on the explosion that had taken Angela's life, the package that had been delivered, and questions that were begging to be answered.

In the aftermath of a devastating home explosion that claims the life of Angela, seasoned Detective Winston hones in on two prime suspects: Patrick and Alvin.

Detective Winston winced a little as he pulled up to Angela's home. What was once a well kept, welcoming residence was now charred remains. All due to an explosion powerful enough to shake the neighborhood. As he began his investigation into the events leading up to the incident, one name kept surfacing: Patrick, local surfing instructor and part-time demolition worker who frequently had to handle, use, and was often training on disposing explosives at his job as a requirement of safety measures.
 
To understand this suspect more, Winston set off to meet the man at his next surfing lesson. Under the blistering sun, Patrick was there, quick to anger, bellowing at his students who seemed more frightened than focused on the waves. Several students have had grievances about his harsh teaching methods, which translated to Winston as a lack of patience.

When the session started, Winston noticed the scar that ran down the side of his face which looked ill-treated. Patrick noticed him too. His tall and sturdy figure smirked and sauntered towards Winston. "Detective, right?" his voice was rough, like sandpaper against a rough surface. "Heard about Angela, disturbing really." 

Patrick's nonchalance bothered Winston, but he gave an understanding nod. "Yeah, it is. You were doing demolition work part-time, handling and using explosives, and even have been frequently training on disposing of them, right? That could surely be a dangerous work, isn't it?" Winston queried.

"Sure is," Patrick answered, side-glancing towards his students who were still trying to catch a wave, "Just like surfing, you know, it's all about control." 

Later, Winston found out from the old records that Patrick once worked in a prison. An inmate had assaulted him, and despite being injured, he'd managed to subdue the prisoner. The incident had left him off fieldwork due to minor injuries, but his bravery had been noted. 

Winston also learned that Patrick borrowed a large sum of money from Angela. A neighbor heard Angela frequently threatening to call the cops on Patrick, but he was always around. Patrick had been seen near Angela's home that evening, the very scene of the explosion. There were no others found in the vicinity at the time.

Now, it seemed Winston was dealing with a surfing instructor who vented his frustrations on his students, an injured prison-personnel-turned-demolition-worker with frequent training on handling and disposing explosives who borrowed heavily from a woman who is now dead and was glimpsed around her house before the explosion. Interesting, certainly, but Winston knew there was more to uncover before any real pieces could begin to fall into place here. This was just the start.

Winston sat in his car, surveying through the battered fence that surrounded Angela's suburban home. The yellow tape marking off the scene of the crime fluttered eerily in the wind. Within that marked perimeter was devastation... an explosion had taken place there recently.

As Winston stepped out of his vehicle, a mail truck adorned with cheerful, vibrant colors pulled up to a house down the street. It was Alvin, a well-liked figure in the community, known best for his calm demeanor and reliability. Ex-military, he was now a delivery man and today, just like every day, he was doing his rounds. Along with the rumors of Alvin's unusual fascination with Angela and his tendency to lurk outside her home during unexpected hours, several witnesses had observed Alvin frequently retreating to his garage, where he kept a collection of various artifacts, including explosives and old photos of Angela.

Alvin had scheduled stops all over the neighborhood, but Angela - the victim in Winston's case - was one that he had on his list daily. It was on Alvin's delivery sheet that day too - a package was scheduled for Angela's house. Always punctual, Alvin would hand-deliver packages to Angela; she was always home to receive them, waiting for him at her front door with a box of his old photos of her flashed to Alvin’s mind. 

Angela's old housekeeper clued Winston in on something else. She sat, frail and teary-eyed, as she told him that Angela had recently filed a restraining order against Alvin. Despite this, he continued to visit her home with deliveries daily, revealing a persistence that bordered on stalking. 

"I learned about a lot of things in the army, Winston. How to survive on tinned beans, how to make a fire, how to assemble a rifle... Yes, I might have learnt a bit about explosives too, and have some at my place, but they're never intended for any harm," Alvin responds, visibly tense.

Winston catches sight of the mail truck and the single, small box addressed to Angela seated in the front. It was clear the last delivery of the day was made to her and it was also known that Angela was there to receive it. Angela's neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, a nosy old lady who saw everything on the block had testified to Angela personally receiving the parcel at around the same time the explosion incident occurred.

Long after Winston had left, Alvin continued to stare at the spot where Winston had been sitting, his calm exterior shattered. With dread, he remembered the package marked "explosive" in his garage, along with a stack of Angela's old photos, and the parcel he had delivered just days before Angela's house had gone up in flames.

In the quiet crevices of a local library, Stephen's life came to an abrupt end, impaled by a trident; now, it's up to the tenacious Detective Winston to unravel the mystery and discern if Sophie or Lowell are responsible.

After another tiring day of working the case, Winston parked his car in a quiet, dimly lit street outside of a popular local gym. Inside was Sophie, his latest person of interest, who had gained notoriety for expressing racist viewpoints at several social gatherings. Witnesses and victims had come forth, stating that Sophie, in her fury, had confronted and threatened individuals belonging to the groups she so openly expressed prejudice against.

Sophie, who was known for her athletic prowess as a professional trident thrower, was amid an intense workout when Winston entered the facility. She was preparing for an upcoming competition, her muscles rippling under the strain of each precise throw. Her unlimited access to the gym's professional equipment made this process much easier.

Winston approached her once she finished her practice throws. "Ms. Sophie," he greeted, his gaze unwavering.

She turned, her eyes blazing with a competitive energy. "Detective Winston," she replied. "Can I help you?"

"Maybe. I'm asking around about a gym guest, Stephen. He was part of your clientele, wasn't he?" He knew the answer, having found that Stephen visited this gym regularly.

Sophie's expression hardened. "Yes," she confirmed. "So what?"

"Stephen has been murdered in the library downtown." Winston noticed Sophie's eyes flicker with surprise, or guilt perhaps. Sophie knew Stephen's routine well. His unusual, long hours spent at the library coincided with the time of the crime, a detail Sophie was well aware of. 

Sophie looked genuinely shocked. "Library?" she echoed, her brows furrowing.

"Yes, the library. Quite an unusual scene, isn't it? Especially when we found a trident near his body. It happens to be identical to the kind here in your gym," Winston added.

Immediately, Sophie blanched. She swiveled her head towards the impressive array of trident equipment, nervously mimicking a laugh. “A trident?” she repeated, “Yes… we do have tridents here for… for our clients.”

Winston changed his line of questioning. "Stephen belonged to a particular minority group, didn't he? One I've heard which you've openly threatened and discriminated against at several social events. Isn't that so?"

Sophie, visibly taken aback, struggled to reply, "I...I have...expressed my views at some social gatherings," she stammered out, her face reddening. "But what's that got to do with Stephen?"

Winston leaned back in his chair and swiveled around to view the wall behind him. There, pinned up in a chaotic array of incident reports, photographs, and clipped newspaper articles, was the ever-growing puzzle that was Stuart's life - and brutal death.

Stuart was no saint. A frequent visitor of weekly wrestling matches, he was well-known for his affinity for the ring's harsh lights and the electrifying atmosphere. He wasn't just a wrestling fan. Stuart was a former drug runner, who narrowly escaped the long arm of the law. He gave up drug smuggling after his last run-in with the cops; a move that caused a few raised eyebrows among his associates.

Winston swiveled back to his desk and picked up Octavia's prison file. Octavia was no saint either. Despite being behind bars, she was a constant thorn in the prison warden's strict regimen. She was seen trying to steal drugs from the medical ward just last month, and was found alone in her cell during Stuart's murder. The lack of commotion in the prison that day as recorded by their intensive CCTV coverage was highly suspect. 

The detective further examined the prisoner's file, scrutinizing the day-release pass she received for the wrestling event. The warden's signature was clearly visible on the pass. Evidently, Octavia was granted a rare liberty; she was allowed to join one of the wrestling matches - the same event where Stuart was found lifeless.

However, there was no apparent reason why Octavia would want drugs. She had no history of fancying them recreationally, and the prison file showed no signs of any mental illnesses that might have explained her erratic behavior. But it was clear as day that she was in constant turmoil without drugs. The file also covered various incidents where her withdrawal symptoms were reported.

Winston sighed as he put down Octavia's file, rubbing his temples wearily. The case was a complicated one, filled with numerous possible explanations, but no definite answers. He needed a good night's rest; tomorrow was another day of work. So, he turned off the desk lamp and disappeared into the darkness of the night.

Winston lounged back in his old leather chair, scanning the sparse details about the victim, Stuart. Another death in the wrestling ring, another round of evidence to collect and people to interrogate. The lead pipe responsible for Stuart's demise remained at the forefront of Winston's thoughts. But this investigation was unique. His present interviewee, a staunchly religious man by the name of Shawn, was not just any ordinary spectator.

Shawn was known by many in the community. A Theologian of some hard-core sect of Christianity, he was often seen after wrestling matches, conducting sermons in the ring and preaching to his followers or buried in books. On the night of the murder, he was no different. Winston found Shawn at the church, where he had returned to refine the sermon he had delivered after the match that fateful night.

"I understand that you conducted a sermon at the wrestling ring just around the time of Stuart's death," Winston began.

Shawn's eyes glinted with sadness as he responded, "Yes, that's correct. Stuart had even attended these after-match sermons sometimes. He was going through some tough times and often confided in me." 

"And you were there post-match, conducting the sermon when it all happened?" asked Winston. "Well, wrestling matches usually wrap up late, so my sermon would have been around the approximate time of...you know," Shawn trailed off, unable to speak about the tragedy.

Rest of the story remains the same.

In the eerie silence of a wrestling ring, Stuart's life was brutally ended with a lead pipe, leaving Detective Winston with a chilling case and two prime suspects: Shawn and Octavia.

Winston sat on the bench outside the state penitentiary, going over the leviathan-sized stack of Octavia's prison records, flicking out the pages one by one. They depicted the daily life of a woman maintaining an intense physical regimen. She was fit, she was disciplined. A disciplined, successful wrestler.

The sun faded into the horizon as he stared at the record of the wrestling event Octavia had been part of and for which she had been granted a day-release pass. The sign-off from the warden stood out even in the dimming twilight. In Winston's years of experience, it was a rare thing for a prisoner to be given such a privilege, but to wrestle? That was unheard of.

Octavia, however, was an exception. She reportedly kept up her wrestling training in prison, rigorously keeping in shape. This explained her winning streak in the prison's wrestling records. But it didn't explain everything.

A chill wind swept through the yard and Winston flipped a page, his eyes catching on a note about Octavia's disciplinary actions. Several infractions, including her use of illegal foreign objects in wrestling matches, her attacks on other inmates – even using a tray as a weapon once – were duly noted.

It was the mention of her being caught as she attempted to steal from the prison’s medical ward though, that drew Winston's attention back. This was a woman fighting, desperate even, against the grips of drug addiction. Withdrawal symptoms were known to be brutal, but rarely did prisoners resort to such extreme measures.

Moving next to Stuart's file, it was clear his troubles began long before his death. Notorious from his time smuggling drugs, he later succumbed to the law's pressure and put a stop to his operations. It was a known fact he later became a regular at wrestling events, noticing Octavia there more than once. A rehabilitation, or an escape, who could tell?

Whether his love for wrestling drew him into proximity with Octavia, or his previous life of drug-running played a part, was unclear. But while drug addiction had inflamed Octavia’s desire for the substances Stuart had dealt in his past, she too shared a passion for the wrestling spectacles for which he was known. Their paths certainly crossed more than once on wrestling's squared circle.

As Winston compiled his notes, having immersed himself in the life histories of both Stuart and Octavia, he felt a strange connection between them. The pieces were there. Now, he just had to fit them together into a telling tale of how this wrestling ring turned into a crime scene, and transformed a fit, strong woman into a suspect.

Shawn's home was an impressive sight, and the library even more so. Winston noticed it immediately upon walking in, walls nearly toppling over with books. A slight air of dust hung in the quiet, still air of the room. Some of the book spines jumped out at him - collections of works on serial killers - but he reminded himself to stay focused on his task at hand.

"Detective Winston," Shawn greeted him, rising on his entry, "Please have a seat." 

"Thank you, Shawn," Winston complied, glancing about the room. “Impressive library. Do a lot of your work in here?” 

Shawn nodded, gesturing around the room, "Yes, my sermons take a lot out of me, and preparation requires time. I often seclude myself in my study, preparing for my sermons. My faith is the core of my being, detective.” 

Winston nodded, listening to Shawn talk proudly about his devotion to his faith. He did not interrupt when Shawn spoke of his religious rituals involving lead pipes that he had been taught by elders of his faith. 

Shawn leaned back in his armchair, wiping a bead of sweat from his forehead, "In fact, detective, on the night of the incident, I was conducting a sermon for our group, right here in my home study, followed by our ritual at the wrestling field. Stuart solicited my presence to view the wrestling match and then to conduct the closing rituals."

"And how do you normally feel after these rituals? You look a bit tired, Shawn," Winston softly asked.

Shawn rubbed his eyes and sighed, "Studying and my religious work often tire me. It's a lot of late nights, yes..."

Winston nodded and stood up to leave, "I appreciate you taking the time to chat with me, Shawn. I'm sorry for your loss." 

Shawn thanked him and Winston left, noting the enclosing quiet of the study once more before he did. The library lingered in his mind, but he shut that thought away as he walked out of the house.
